title: Der Teufel und seine Großmutter
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 125. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, thaten). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 125 opens on three deserting soldiers hiding from the army in a cornfield, starving, who sell themselves to the Devil for seven years of plenty on the condition that they solve a riddle at the end or lose their souls. One of them finds the Devil's own grandmother, who hides him and overhears the answer, letting all three walk free with a whip that conjures money whenever they crack it.

sentences.t: Es war ein großer Krieg, und der König hatte viel Soldaten, gab ihnen aber wenig Sold, so daß sie nicht davon leben konnten.
sentences.l: There was a great war, and the king had many soldiers, gave them however little pay, so that they could not live from it.
sentences.i: There was a great war, and the king had many soldiers, but he gave them little pay, so that they could not live on it.
sentences.n: Soldaten and Sold are the same word at root — a soldier is a man who is paid — and the tale sets the two side by side in its first sentence. viel stands uninflected before a plural, an older usage. The second clause drops its subject er. The shared glossary marks soldaten as Low German; this tale is High German throughout, and the entry is corrected here. The 1857 edition gives this tale no paragraphs at all; the ones here were put in for the sake of reading it on a screen, and nothing but the spacing is new.

sentences.t: Da thaten sich drei zusammen und wollten ausreißen.
sentences.l: Then three did themselves together and wanted to run away.
sentences.i: So three of them banded together and meant to desert.
sentences.n: sich zusammenthun is to band together; thaten is the 1857 spelling of taten, from thun (modern tun). ausreißen is literally to tear oneself out, and of a soldier it is to desert.

sentences.t: Einer sprach zum andern „wenn wir erwischt werden, so hängt man uns an den Galgenbaum: wie wollen wirs machen?“
sentences.l: One said to the other “if we are caught, then one hangs us on the gallows-tree: how will we do it?”
sentences.i: One said to the other, “If we are caught they will hang us on the gallows tree — how shall we set about it?”
sentences.n: man is the impersonal “one”, where English prefers a vague “they”. wirs is wir es. der Galgenbaum, the gallows-tree, is the older and grimmer word for the gallows.

sentences.t: Sprach der andere „seht dort das große Kornfeld, wenn wir uns da verstecken, so findet uns kein Mensch: das Heer darf nicht hinein und muß morgen weiter ziehen.“
sentences.l: Said the other “see there the great cornfield, if we hide ourselves there, then no person finds us: the army may not go in and must move on tomorrow.”
sentences.i: The other said, “Look there at the great cornfield — if we hide in it, not a soul will find us; the army is not allowed in, and must move on tomorrow.”
sentences.n: Sprach der andere begins with its verb, a narrative turn this tale uses over and over when the speaker changes. kein Mensch is the everyday “not a soul”. darf nicht hinein has no verb of motion at all: the hinein carries it. weiter ziehen, of an army, is to march on.

sentences.t: Sie krochen in das Korn, aber das Heer zog nicht weiter, sondern blieb rund herum liegen.
sentences.l: They crept into the corn, but the army did not move on, but rather stayed lying round about.
sentences.i: They crept into the corn, but the army did not march on; it stayed encamped all around.
sentences.n: liegen bleiben, of an army, is to stay put, to remain encamped. rund herum is “round about”. sondern is the “but” that must follow a negative.

sentences.t: Sie saßen zwei Tage und zwei Nächte im Korn und hatten so großen Hunger daß sie beinah gestorben wären: giengen sie aber heraus, so war ihnen der Tod gewis.
sentences.l: They sat two days and two nights in the corn and had such great hunger that they would almost have died: but if they went out, then death was certain to them.
sentences.i: They sat two days and two nights in the corn, and were so hungry that they nearly died of it; but if they came out, death was certain.
sentences.n: Hunger haben is how German says to be hungry. wären gestorben is the subjunctive of what almost happened. giengen sie aber heraus is a conditional made by putting the verb first, with no wenn. gewis is the 1857 spelling of gewiss, and ihnen is the dative of the people concerned.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie „was hilft uns unser Ausreißen, wir müssen hier elendig sterben.“
sentences.l: Then they said “what helps us our running-away, we must die here miserably.”
sentences.i: Then they said, “What good is our deserting to us? We must die here in misery.”
sentences.n: was hilft uns … is a question that expects the answer “nothing”. das Ausreißen is the infinitive used as a noun, the act of running away. elendig is an older form of elend, wretched.

sentences.t: Indem kam ein feuriger Drache durch die Luft geflogen, der senkte sich zu ihnen herab und fragte sie warum sie sich da versteckt hätten.
sentences.l: Just then came a fiery dragon flying through the air, that lowered itself down to them and asked them why they had hidden themselves there.
sentences.i: Just then a fiery dragon came flying through the air; it sank down to them and asked why they had hidden themselves there.
sentences.n: indem here is the older “just then, meanwhile”, not the modern “by doing”. kam … geflogen, “came flying”, is the ordinary German way of joining motion to manner. der is a demonstrative picking up the dragon where English would start again with “it”. hätten keeps the question as the dragon’s own.

sentences.t: Sie antworteten „wir sind drei Soldaten, und sind ausgerissen weil unser Sold gering war:
sentences.l: They answered “we are three soldiers, and have run away because our pay was small:
sentences.i: They answered, “We are three soldiers, and we have deserted because our pay was too little;
sentences.n: sind ausgerissen forms its perfect with sein, as German does for verbs of motion and change of state. gering is small in amount, meagre. The colon does the work of a semicolon.

sentences.t: nun müssen wir hier Hungers sterben, wenn wir liegen bleiben, oder wir müssen am Galgen baumeln, wenn wir heraus gehen.“
sentences.l: now we must die here of hunger, if we stay lying, or we must dangle on the gallows, if we go out.”
sentences.i: now we must either starve here if we stay lying low, or dangle on the gallows if we come out.”
sentences.n: Hungers is an old genitive of cause, to die of hunger. liegen bleiben, of men in hiding, is to stay put. baumeln is to dangle, and am Galgen baumeln is the soldiers’ own word for being hanged.

sentences.t: „Wollt ihr mir sieben Jahre dienen,“ sagte der Drache, „so will ich euch mitten durchs Heer führen, daß euch niemand erwischen soll?“
sentences.l: “Will you serve me seven years,” said the dragon, “then I will lead you right through the middle of the army, so that no one shall catch you?”
sentences.i: “If you will serve me seven years,” said the dragon, “I will carry you right through the middle of the army, so that no one shall catch you.”
sentences.n: Wollt ihr … with the verb first is a conditional, “if you will”, and the so that follows is “then”. dienen takes the dative, mir. The 1857 text closes with a question mark though the sentence has turned into a statement: the bargain is put as a question.

sentences.t: „Wir haben keine Wahl und müssens annehmen“ antworteten sie.
sentences.l: “We have no choice and must accept it” they answered.
sentences.i: “We have no choice; we must take it,” they answered.
sentences.n: müssens is müssen es, the es standing for the offer. annehmen is separable, but after a modal the infinitive keeps its particle attached.

sentences.t: Da packte sie der Drache in seine Klauen, führte sie durch die Luft über das Heer hinweg und setzte sie weit davon wieder auf die Erde; der Drache war aber niemand als der Teufel.
sentences.l: Then the dragon seized them in his claws, carried them through the air away over the army and set them far from it down again on the earth; the dragon however was no one but the devil.
sentences.i: Then the dragon seized them in his claws, carried them through the air away over the army, and set them down on the ground again far beyond it; but the dragon was none other than the devil.
sentences.n: The object sie stands before the subject der Drache — the case endings, not the order, say who seizes whom. hinweg über etwas is away over something. setzte is transitive here, to set something down; the shared glossary answers this spelling with reflexive sich setzen, to sit down, and the entry is corrected for this tale. niemand als is “none other than”, and the tale gives the game away in the middle of a sentence.

sentences.t: Er gab ihnen ein kleines Peitschchen und sprach „peitscht und knallt ihr damit, so wird so viel Geld vor euch herum springen als ihr verlangt:
sentences.l: He gave them a little whip and said “if you whip and crack with it, then as much money will spring about before you as you demand:
sentences.i: He gave them a little whip and said, “Whip and crack with it, and as much money will fly about before you as you ask for;
sentences.n: Peitschchen is the diminutive of die Peitsche, a whip; the doubled chch is what happens when the ending -chen meets a stem ending in -sch. peitscht und knallt ihr damit is another verb-first conditional. verlangt is second person plural here, “you ask for”; the shared glossary gives it as a past participle and the entry is corrected.

sentences.t: ihr könnt dann wie große Herrn leben, Pferde halten und in Wagen fahren:
sentences.l: you can then live like great lords, keep horses and drive in carriages:
sentences.i: then you may live like great lords, keep horses and ride in carriages;
sentences.n: Herrn is the older short plural of Herr. Pferde halten is to keep horses as one keeps a household, and in Wagen fahren is to go about by carriage — the two marks of a gentleman.

sentences.t: nach Verlauf der sieben Jahre aber seid ihr mein eigen.“
sentences.l: after the course of the seven years however you are my own.”
sentences.i: but when the seven years have run out, you are my own.”
sentences.n: nach Verlauf + genitive is “at the expiry of”. mein eigen stands uninflected, an old fixed way of saying “my own property”. The present seid does duty for the future, as German lets it.

sentences.t: Dann hielt er ihnen ein Buch vor, in das mußten sie sich alle drei unterschreiben.
sentences.l: Then he held out to them a book, in which all three had to sign themselves.
sentences.i: Then he held a book out to them, and all three had to write their names in it.
sentences.n: vorhalten, to hold something out in front of someone, is separable: hielt … vor. sich unterschreiben is to sign oneself, that is, to bind oneself in writing; the signature is the whole contract.

sentences.t: „Doch will ich euch,“ sprach er, „erst noch ein Räthsel aufgeben, könnt ihr das rathen, sollt ihr frei sein und aus meiner Gewalt entlassen.“
sentences.l: “Yet will I to you,” he said, “first set a riddle, if you can guess it, you shall be free and released from my power.”
sentences.i: “But first,” he said, “I will set you a riddle; if you can guess it, you shall be free and released out of my power.”
sentences.n: ein Räthsel aufgeben is to set a riddle; Räthsel is the 1857 spelling of Rätsel. rathen (modern raten) serves both for advising and for guessing. könnt ihr das rathen is once again a verb-first conditional. entlassen hangs on the sollt ihr sein of the clause before.

sentences.t: Da flog der Drache von ihnen weg, und sie reisten fort mit ihren Peitschchen, hatten Geld die Fülle, ließen sich Herrenkleider machen und zogen in der Welt herum.
sentences.l: Then the dragon flew away from them, and they travelled off with their little whips, had money in abundance, had lordly clothes made for themselves and roamed about in the world.
sentences.i: Then the dragon flew away from them, and they set off with their little whips, with money in plenty; they had gentlemen’s clothes made for themselves and went roaming about the world.
sentences.n: Geld die Fülle is an old turn of phrase, money to the full. sich etwas machen lassen is to have something made for oneself; the shared glossary answers ließen with quite another phrase and is corrected here. herumziehen, to roam about, is separable, and the shared entry for zogen carries another tale’s sense, so that one is corrected too.

sentences.t: Wo sie waren, lebten sie in Freuden und Herrlichkeit, fuhren mit Pferden und Wagen, aßen und tranken, thaten aber nichts Böses.
sentences.l: Wherever they were, they lived in joys and splendour, drove with horses and carriage, ate and drank, but did nothing evil.
sentences.i: Wherever they were they lived in joy and splendour, went about with horses and carriage, ate and drank — and did nothing wicked.
sentences.n: wo here is “wherever”. in Freuden is a set dative plural, “in joys”. nichts Böses capitalises the adjective because it stands as a noun. The line settles quietly what kind of men these are, which is what the end of the tale rests on.

sentences.t: Die Zeit verstrich ihnen schnell, und als es mit den sieben Jahren zu Ende gieng, ward zweien gewaltig angst und bang,
sentences.l: The time slipped away for them quickly, and when it was going to an end with the seven years, two of them grew mightily fearful and afraid,
sentences.i: The time slipped away quickly for them, and as the seven years drew towards their end, two of them grew sick with dread,
sentences.n: ihnen is the dative of the people concerned: the time passed for them. zu Ende gehen is to draw to an end. einem wird angst und bang is an impersonal idiom with the person in the dative — zweien, “to two of them” — and angst und bang is a fixed pair, dread doubled. The shared glossary marks bang as Low German, but this is the High German idiom, and the entry is corrected here.

sentences.t: der dritte aber nahms auf die leichte Schulter und sprach „Brüder, fürchtet nichts, ich bin nicht auf den Kopf gefallen, ich errathe das Räthsel.“
sentences.l: the third however took it on the light shoulder and said “brothers, fear nothing, I am not fallen on the head, I shall guess the riddle.”
sentences.i: but the third took it lightly and said, “Brothers, fear nothing; I was not dropped on my head — I shall guess the riddle.”
sentences.n: etwas auf die leichte Schulter nehmen, to take a thing on the light shoulder, is to make light of it, and the phrase is still current. nicht auf den Kopf gefallen sein, not to have fallen on one’s head, is to be no fool. errathe is a present standing for the future — the confidence is the point. fürchtet is the imperative to more than one.

sentences.t: Sie giengen hinaus aufs Feld, saßen da und die zwei machten betrübte Gesichter.
sentences.l: They went out onto the field, sat there and the two made troubled faces.
sentences.i: They went out into the field and sat there, and the two of them pulled long faces.
sentences.n: aufs is auf das. ein Gesicht machen is to put on a face, to look a certain way. betrübt is grieved, downcast.

sentences.t: Da kam eine alte Frau daher, die fragte warum sie so traurig wären.
sentences.l: Then an old woman came along, she asked why they were so sad.
sentences.n: daher kommen is to come along. die is a demonstrative, “she”, picking the woman up rather than opening a relative clause. wären keeps the question hers rather than the narrator’s.

sentences.t: „Ach, was liegt euch daran, ihr könnt uns doch nicht helfen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, what lies to you at it, you cannot help us anyway.”
sentences.i: “Oh, what does it matter to you? You cannot help us anyway.”
sentences.n: an etwas liegen is impersonal with the person in the dative: was liegt euch daran, what is it to you. doch is the flavouring particle of resignation, “anyway, after all”. The speech has no tag at all — the quotation marks do the work.

sentences.t: „Wer weiß,“ antwortete sie, „vertraut mir nur euern Kummer.“
sentences.l: “Who knows,” she answered, “only confide to me your trouble.”
sentences.i: “Who knows,” she answered; “only tell me your trouble.”
sentences.n: weiß here is the verb wissen, to know — not the adjective weiß, white, which is what the shared glossary answers this spelling with; the entry is corrected for this tale. vertraut is the imperative to more than one, from vertrauen, to entrust, and that entry is corrected as well. euern is the 1857 form of euren.

sentences.t: Da erzählten sie ihr sie wären des Teufels Diener gewesen, fast sieben Jahre lang, der hätte ihnen Geld wie Heu geschafft,
sentences.l: Then they told her they had been the devil’s servants, almost seven years long, he had got them money like hay,
sentences.i: So they told her that they had been the devil’s servants for almost seven years, and that he had got them money like hay,
sentences.n: The whole telling stands in the subjunctive — wären, hätte — which is how German marks reported speech, with no daß needed. Geld wie Heu is a set comparison: money in heaps, as hay is heaped. der is once more a demonstrative, here for the devil.

sentences.t: sie hätten sich ihm aber verschrieben, und wären ihm verfallen, wenn sie nach den sieben Jahren nicht ein Räthsel auflösen könnten.
sentences.l: but they had signed themselves over to him, and would be forfeit to him, if they could not solve a riddle after the seven years.
sentences.i: but that they had signed themselves over to him, and would fall to him, if after the seven years they could not solve a riddle.
sentences.n: sich jemandem verschreiben is to make oneself over to someone in writing — the book they signed. jemandem verfallen sein is to be forfeit to someone when the term lapses. ein Räthsel auflösen is to solve a riddle; the noun die Auflösung, the solution, comes back later in the tale.

sentences.t: Die Alte sprach, „soll euch geholfen werden, so muß einer von euch in den Wald gehen,
sentences.l: The old woman said, “if you are to be helped, then one of you must go into the forest,
sentences.n: die Alte is an adjective used as a noun, “the old woman”. soll euch geholfen werden is an impersonal passive with the verb first, which makes it conditional: “if help is to come to you”; helfen takes the dative, so euch cannot simply become an English subject.

sentences.t: da wird er an eine eingestürzte Felsenwand kommen, die aussieht wie ein Häuschen, in das muß er eintreten, dann wird er Hilfe finden.“
sentences.l: there he will come to a fallen-in rock face, that looks like a little house, into that he must step, then he will find help.”
sentences.i: there he will come to a rock face fallen in on itself, which looks like a little house; into that he must go, and then he will find help.”
sentences.n: einstürzen is to cave in; eingestürzt describes the rock as having fallen in on itself. in das is a demonstrative standing first, “into that”, so the verb comes before its subject: muß er eintreten.

sentences.t: Die zwei traurigen dachten „das wird uns doch nicht retten,“ und blieben sitzen, der dritte aber, der lustige, machte sich auf und gieng so weit in den Wald, bis er die Felsenhütte fand.
sentences.l: The two sad ones thought “that will surely not save us,” and stayed sitting, the third however, the merry one, set himself out and went so far into the forest until he found the rock hut.
sentences.i: The two sad ones thought, “That will never save us,” and stayed sitting; but the third, the merry one, set out and went so far into the forest that he found the rock hut.
sentences.n: die zwei traurigen and der lustige are adjectives used as nouns, the tale’s shorthand for the three men. sitzen bleiben is to stay sitting. sich aufmachen is to set out, and its auf goes to the end. so weit … bis, “so far … until”, is where English says “so far that”.

sentences.t: In dem Häuschen aber saß eine steinalte Frau, die war des Teufels Großmutter, und fragte ihn woher er käme und was er hier wollte.
sentences.l: In the little house however sat a stone-old woman, she was the devil’s grandmother, and asked him from where he came and what he wanted here.
sentences.i: But in the little house sat an ancient woman; she was the devil’s grandmother, and she asked him where he came from and what he wanted here.
sentences.n: steinalt, stone-old, is the ordinary German for very old indeed. des Teufels Großmutter puts the genitive first, an older order that English keeps in “the devil’s grandmother”. käme and wollte are the subjunctives of her questions.

sentences.t: Er erzählte ihr alles, was geschehen war, und weil er ihr wohl gefiel, hatte sie Erbarmen und sagte sie wollte ihm helfen.
sentences.l: He told her everything that had happened, and because he pleased her well, she had pity and said she wanted to help him.
sentences.i: He told her everything that had happened, and because he pleased her well, she took pity and said she would help him.
sentences.n: gefallen takes the dative of the person pleased: er gefiel ihr — German makes the pleasing thing the subject. Erbarmen haben is to have pity. wollte in reported speech is “would”, her promise rather than her wish.

sentences.t: Sie hob einen großen Stein auf, der über einem Keller lag, und sagte „da verstecke dich, du kannst alles hören was hier gesprochen wird, sitz nur still und rege dich nicht:
sentences.l: She lifted up a great stone that lay over a cellar, and said “hide yourself there, you can hear everything that is spoken here, only sit still and do not stir yourself:
sentences.i: She lifted up a great stone that lay over a cellar and said, “Hide yourself in there; you can hear everything that is said here — only sit still and do not stir;
sentences.n: aufheben is separable: hob … auf. verstecke, sitz and rege are all imperatives to one person; the shared glossary answers sitz with the mounting of a horse and rege with an adjective, and both entries are corrected for this tale. sich regen is to stir at all. nur softens a command to “just, only”.

sentences.t: wann der Drache kommt, will ich ihn wegen der Räthsel befragen: mir sagt er alles; und dann achte auf das was er antwortet.“
sentences.l: when the dragon comes, I will question him about the riddles: to me he tells everything; and then pay heed to what he answers.”
sentences.i: when the dragon comes I will question him about the riddles — he tells me everything — and then take heed of what he answers.”
sentences.n: wann stands here in the older sense of wenn, “when, once”. befragen, to question someone, takes wegen with the genitive for the matter asked about. mir sagt er alles puts the dative first for weight. achte is an imperative, and achten auf takes the accusative; the shared entry gives a different construction and is corrected here.

sentences.t: Um zwölf Uhr Nachts kam der Drache angeflogen und verlangte sein Essen.
sentences.l: At twelve o’clock at night the dragon came flying up and demanded his food.
sentences.i: At twelve o’clock at night the dragon came flying in and demanded his supper.
sentences.n: Nachts is an adverbial genitive, “of a night”. kam angeflogen is the same “came flying” pattern as at his first appearance. das Essen is the meal itself, the infinitive used as a noun.

sentences.t: Die Großmutter deckte den Tisch und trug Trank und Speise auf, daß er vergnügt war, und sie aßen und tranken zusammen.
sentences.l: The grandmother laid the table and carried up drink and food, so that he was content, and they ate and drank together.
sentences.i: The grandmother laid the table and served up drink and food, so that he was well pleased, and they ate and drank together.
sentences.n: den Tisch decken is to lay the table. auftragen, to serve up, is separable: trug … auf. Trank is the noun here, a drink or draught — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the past tense of trinken, and the entry is corrected for this tale. Trank und Speise is an old paired phrase, drink and meat.

sentences.t: Da fragte sie ihn im Gespräch wies den Tag ergangen wäre, und wie viel Seelen er kriegt hätte.
sentences.l: Then she asked him in conversation how it had gone that day, and how many souls he had got.
sentences.i: Then in the course of talk she asked him how the day had gone with him, and how many souls he had got.
sentences.n: wies is wie es. es ergeht jemandem is impersonal, “things go for someone”, with the person in the dative; den Tag is an accusative of time, during the day. Seelen are what the devil is collecting, and the tale keeps the accounting flat and plain.

sentences.t: „Es wollte mir heute nicht recht glücken,“ antwortete er, „aber ich habe drei Soldaten gepackt, die sind mir sicher.“
sentences.l: “It would not quite succeed for me today,” he answered, “but I have seized three soldiers, they are certain to me.”
sentences.i: “It would not go quite right for me today,” he answered, “but I have got hold of three soldiers — those are safe in my hands.”
sentences.n: es will mir nicht glücken is impersonal with the person in the dative: things will not come off for me. recht here is “quite, properly”. die sind mir sicher is the dative again, “sure for me” — he cannot lose them.

sentences.t: „Ja, drei Soldaten,“ sagte sie, „die haben etwas an sich, die können dir noch entkommen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, three soldiers,” she said, “those have something about them, those can still escape you.”
sentences.i: “Yes, three soldiers,” she said, “there is something about those — they may escape you yet.”
sentences.n: etwas an sich haben is to have something about one, a quality not named. die at the head of both clauses is a demonstrative, “those ones”. entkommen takes the dative, dir. She is baiting him, and it works at once.

sentences.t: Sprach der Teufel höhnisch „die sind mein, denen gebe ich noch ein Räthsel auf, das sie nimmermehr rathen können.“
sentences.l: Said the devil scornfully “those are mine, to those I set yet a riddle that they can nevermore guess.”
sentences.i: The devil said scornfully, “Those are mine; I will set them a riddle they can never in the world guess.”
sentences.n: denen is the dative plural of the demonstrative, “to those ones”, and stands first in its clause. aufgeben is separable: gebe … auf, with the auf waiting at the end. nimmermehr is a never with no way round it.

sentences.t: „Was ist das für ein Räthsel?“ fragte sie.
sentences.l: “What is that for a riddle?” she asked.
sentences.i: “What sort of a riddle is that?” she asked.
sentences.n: was für ein is the fixed phrase for “what kind of”; für does not mean “for” here, and the two halves may stand apart, as they do in the answers later.

sentences.t: „Das will ich dir sagen: in der großen Nordsee liegt eine todte Meerkatze, das soll ihr Braten sein:
sentences.l: “That will I tell you: in the great North Sea lies a dead long-tailed monkey, that shall be their roast:
sentences.i: “That I will tell you: in the great North Sea there lies a dead monkey — that shall be their roast;
sentences.n: todte is the adjective dead, in the 1857 spelling of tote; the shared glossary answers this spelling with the noun der Todte, a dead man, and the entry is corrected for this tale. die Meerkatze is a long-tailed monkey, and the word is built from Meer, sea, and Katze, cat — which is how it comes to be dredged up out of the North Sea. Braten is the noun, a roast, not the verb braten, and that entry is corrected too.

sentences.t: und von einem Wallfisch die Rippe, das soll ihr silberner Löffel sein:
sentences.l: and from a whale the rib, that shall be their silver spoon:
sentences.i: and a rib from a whale — that shall be their silver spoon;
sentences.n: Wallfisch is the 1857 spelling of Walfisch, a whale. von einem Wallfisch die Rippe puts the owner first and the thing after, an older order. The devil’s bill of fare is a mock feast: every item on it is the wrong size and none of it can be used.

sentences.t: und ein alter hohler Pferdefuß, das soll ihr Weinglas sein.“
sentences.l: and an old hollow horse’s hoof, that shall be their wine glass.”
sentences.n: der Pferdefuß is also the mark by which the devil is known in these tales, one of his feet being a hoof; he is furnishing the table, in a manner of speaking, out of himself.

sentences.t: Als der Teufel zu Bett gegangen war, hob die alte Großmutter den Stein auf und ließ den Soldaten heraus.
sentences.l: When the devil had gone to bed, the old grandmother lifted the stone up and let the soldier out.
sentences.n: zu Bett gehen, with no article, is the fixed phrase. herauslassen is separable, its heraus at the end. gegangen war forms its perfect with sein, as all verbs of motion do.

sentences.t: „Hast du auch alles wohl in Acht genommen?“
sentences.l: “Have you also taken everything well into heed?”
sentences.i: “Did you mark it all well?”
sentences.n: etwas in Acht nehmen is to take note of something, to mind it. auch in a question is not “also” but a check: “did you really?”. wohl here is “well, properly”. She asks without a word of introduction; the 1857 text does not say who is speaking.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach er, „ich weiß genug und will mir schon helfen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” he said, “I know enough and will help myself all right.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “I know enough, and I shall shift for myself.”
sentences.n: weiß is again the verb wissen, not the colour. sich helfen is to manage, to shift for oneself. schon in this position is a promise rather than “already”: it will do.

sentences.t: Darauf mußte er auf einem andern Weg durchs Fenster heimlich und in aller Eile zu seinen Gesellen zurück gehen.
sentences.l: Thereupon he had to go back by another way through the window secretly and in all haste to his companions.
sentences.i: Thereupon he had to go back to his companions by another way, through the window, secretly and in all haste.
sentences.n: darauf is “after that, thereupon”. in aller Eile is a set phrase, in all haste. The 1857 text prints zurück gehen as two words where modern German writes zurückgehen.

sentences.t: Er erzählte ihnen, wie der Teufel von der alten Großmutter wäre überlistet worden und wie er die Auflösung des Räthsels von ihm vernommen hätte.
sentences.l: He told them how the devil had been outwitted by the old grandmother and how he had learned the solution of the riddle from him.
sentences.i: He told them how the devil had been outwitted by the old grandmother, and how he had got the answer to the riddle out of him.
sentences.n: überlisten is to get the better of someone by cunning — die List, a ruse, sits inside the word. wäre überlistet worden is a passive in the subjunctive of reported speech, and von names the doer. vernehmen is to learn or get word of something, more formal than hören.

sentences.t: Da waren sie alle fröhlich und guter Dinge, nahmen die Peitsche und schlugen sich so viel Geld daß es auf der Erde herum sprang.
sentences.l: Then they were all merry and of good things, took the whip and struck themselves so much money that it sprang about on the ground.
sentences.i: Then they were all merry and in good spirits, took the whip and beat out so much money that it went leaping about on the ground.
sentences.n: guter Dinge sein, to be “of good things”, is to be in good spirits — a genitive frozen into an idiom. sich Geld schlagen, to strike money for oneself, is this tale’s own phrase for what the whip does. herumspringen is separable, and sprang stands well away from its herum.

sentences.t: Als die sieben Jahre völlig herum waren, kam der Teufel mit dem Buche, zeigte die Unterschriften und sprach „ich will euch mit in die Hölle nehmen, da sollt ihr eine Mahlzeit haben:
sentences.l: When the seven years were fully round, the devil came with the book, showed the signatures and said “I will take you along with me into hell, there you shall have a meal:
sentences.i: When the seven years were fully up, the devil came with the book, showed them the signatures, and said, “I will take you along with me into hell; there you shall have a meal;
sentences.n: herum sein, of time, is to be up, over. Buche is a dative with the old -e. mitnehmen is separable, and its mit stands far from its verb: will … mit … nehmen. die Hölle is hell itself here; the shared glossary answers it with a tailor’s scrap-drawer from another tale, and the entry is corrected.

sentences.t: könnt ihr mir rathen, was ihr für einen Braten werdet zu essen kriegen, so sollt ihr frei und los sein und dürft auch das Peitschchen behalten.“
sentences.l: if you can tell me what sort of a roast you will get to eat, then you shall be free and loose and may keep the little whip too.”
sentences.i: if you can tell me what sort of roast you will be given to eat, then you shall be free and quit of me, and may keep the little whip as well.”
sentences.n: rathen is to guess here, not to advise. was für einen Braten is again “what sort of”, split around the verb. frei und los sein, free and loose, has the ring of a legal formula: out of the contract altogether.

sentences.t: Da fieng der erste Soldat an „in der großen Nordsee liegt eine todte Meerkatze, das wird wohl der Braten sein.“
sentences.l: Then the first soldier began “in the great North Sea lies a dead long-tailed monkey, that will surely be the roast.”
sentences.i: Then the first soldier began, “In the great North Sea lies a dead monkey — that will be the roast.”
sentences.n: fieng … an is separable anfangen with the particle at the end; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. wohl softens the claim to “I take it, surely”, though he knows quite well that he is right. The answer gives the devil’s own words back almost unchanged, which is the joke.

sentences.t: Der Teufel ärgerte sich, machte „hm! hm! hm!“ und fragte den zweiten „was soll aber euer Löffel sein?“
sentences.l: The devil was annoyed, made “hm! hm! hm!” and asked the second “but what shall your spoon be?”
sentences.i: The devil was vexed, went “hm! hm! hm!”, and asked the second, “But what is your spoon to be?”
sentences.n: sich ärgern is to be annoyed, and is reflexive in German where English has no object at all. machen with a noise is “to go”, as English says a dog goes woof. soll here is “is to be”, the future of an arrangement.

sentences.t: „Von einem Wallfisch die Rippe, das soll unser silberner Löffel sein.“
sentences.l: “From a whale the rib, that shall be our silver spoon.”
sentences.i: “A rib from a whale — that shall be our silver spoon.”
sentences.n: The soldier hands the devil’s phrase back word for word, changing only ihr, their, to unser, our. silberner carries the strong masculine ending because unser itself has none here.

sentences.t: Der Teufel schnitt ein Gesicht, knurrte wieder dreimal „hm! hm! hm!“ und sprach zum dritten „wißt ihr auch was euer Weinglas sein soll?“
sentences.l: The devil cut a face, growled again three times “hm! hm! hm!” and said to the third “do you also know what your wine glass is to be?”
sentences.i: The devil pulled a face, growled three times again, “hm! hm! hm!”, and said to the third, “And do you know what your wine glass is to be?”
sentences.n: ein Gesicht schneiden, to cut a face, is to grimace. wißt is the 1857 spelling of wisst. auch in the question is the same check as before — do you really know?

sentences.t: „Ein alter Pferdefuß, das soll unser Weinglas sein.“
sentences.l: “An old horse’s hoof, that shall be our wine glass.”
sentences.n: The soldier leaves out the devil’s hohler, hollow — the one word of the three answers that does not come back. Nothing in the tale turns on it, and it may be no more than the way a man repeats what he has overheard.

sentences.t: Da flog der Teufel mit einem lauten Schrei fort und hatte keine Gewalt mehr über sie:
sentences.l: Then the devil flew away with a loud cry and had no power any more over them:
sentences.i: Then the devil flew off with a loud shriek, and had no more power over them;
sentences.n: fortfliegen is separable: flog … fort. lauten here is the adjective laut, loud, in the dative — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the verb lauten, to be worded, and schrei with the verb schreien; both entries are corrected for this tale. Gewalt über jemanden haben is to have power over someone.

sentences.t: aber die drei behielten das Peitschchen, schlugen Geld hervor, so viel sie wollten, und lebten vergnügt bis an ihr Ende.
sentences.l: but the three kept the little whip, struck money forth, as much as they wanted, and lived contented until their end.
sentences.i: but the three kept the little whip, beat out as much money as they wanted, and lived content to the end of their days.
sentences.n: hervorschlagen, to strike forth, is separable, and the hervor stands at the end of its clause. bis an ihr Ende is the closing formula, to the end of their lives. Nothing is said of what the signed book might still be worth, and nothing is said of the two who stayed sitting in the field.

glossary.achte: achten — heed, take heed (imperative sg.; achten auf + acc.: to pay heed to)
glossary.alter: alt — old (masc. nom. adj.; ein alter hohler Pferdefuß)
glossary.annehmen: annehmen — to accept, take (an offer) (infinitive; separable an-); also: to take on, engage
glossary.aufgeben: aufgeben — to set (a riddle) (infinitive; separable auf-: ein Räthsel aufgeben); also: to give up
glossary.bang: bang — afraid (in the idiom einem wird angst und bang: dread comes over one; modern bange)
glossary.braten: der Braten — roast, roast meat (also braten: to roast)
glossary.fürchtet: fürchten — fear (imperative pl.; fürchtet nichts: fear nothing)
glossary.gebe: aufgeben — (I) set (a riddle) (1st sg. present; separable auf-: gebe … auf)
glossary.lauten: laut — loud (dat. sg. adj.; mit einem lauten Schrei: with a loud cry)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let, had (something) done (3rd pl. past; sich etwas machen lassen: to have something made)
glossary.pferde: das Pferd — horses (nom./acc. pl.; Pferde halten: to keep horses)
glossary.rathen: rathen — to guess (1857 spelling of raten; ein Räthsel rathen); also: to counsel, advise
glossary.rege: sich regen — stir, move (imperative sg.; rege dich nicht: do not stir)
glossary.schrei: der Schrei — cry, shriek (dat. sg.; also schrei: I cry, from schreien)
glossary.setzte: setzen — set, put down (3rd sg. past, transitive); sich setzen: to sit down
glossary.sitz: sitzen — sit (imperative sg.; sitz still: sit still)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldiers (nom./acc. pl.; High German, not dialect)
glossary.sollt: sollen — you shall, are to (2nd pl. present)
glossary.todte: todt — dead (fem. sg. adj.; 1857 spelling of tot)
glossary.trank: der Trank — drink, draught (acc. sg.; also trank: drank, from trinken)
glossary.verfallen: verfallen — forfeit, fallen due (past part.; jemandem verfallen sein: to be forfeit to someone)
glossary.verlangt: verlangen — demand, ask for (2nd pl. present; also the past participle verlangt)
glossary.vertraut: vertrauen — entrust, confide (imperative pl.; vertraut mir euern Kummer: confide your trouble to me)
glossary.weiß: wissen — know, knows (1st/3rd sg. present); also weiß: white
glossary.zog: ziehen — moved, marched (3rd sg. past; weiter ziehen: to march on); also: pulled
glossary.zogen: ziehen — moved, roamed (3rd pl. past; in der Welt herumziehen: to roam about the world)
